FINDINGS 8.

It is trite that in an eviction petition for bonafide requirement, leave to defend is to be granted only when the tenant is able to raise any triable issue which can be adjudicated only on the consideration of additional evidence.
The tenant must disclose such a prima facie case as would dis-entitle the landlord from obtaining an eviction order, lest an eviction order has to be passed.

Keeping these principles in mind, let us examine if the grounds taken by the RC ARC No. 23/2023 Inderjeet Kaur Vs. Anil Kumar Singhal Page no. 7 of 25 respondent in his leave to defend application, are worthy of trial.

Respondent has denied the existence of any landlord -tenant relationship between the parties.

He alleges petitioner's brother -in- law Mohan Bir Singh to be his landlord and has relied upon some ancient rent receipts and challans of deposit of rent in the Inderjeet Kaur vs Anil Kumar Singhal on 7 March, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/120685659/

Petitioner, on the other hand, has explained as to how she has acquired title in the tenanted premises.

Her parents-in-law were the original owners of the entire property in question i.e.
F14/60-61, Model Town - II of which the tenanted premises F14-61 also forms a part.
They died and left behind petitioner's husband Harjeet Singh Khurana and Mohan Bir Singh as their legal heirs.
The disputes between the brothers were resolved in the High Court in OMP No. 517/2009 dated 05.04.2018.

As per the settlement, the left side of the property which includes the tenanted premises fell into the share of Harjeet Singh Khurana and after his death, same has come to devolve upon her and her children.
In this manner, she has become the co- owner of the tenanted premises.

This left side rear portion is where the tenanted premises is situated and the third party occupant as on date is the respondent in question.

As regards the competence of the petitioner to file the present eviction proceedings, once it is held that she is atleast a co- owner of the tenanted premises, being one of the legal heirs of Harjeet Singh, she is entitled to file the present eviction petition without impleading the other co-owners i.e.
her children.

Reliance in this regard can be placed upon "Dhannalal v. Kalawatibai & Ors.", (2002) 6 SCC 16, wherein it was held that even one co-owner/landlord can file a suit for ejectment against the tenant and it is not necessary that all co-owners/landlords must jointly sue for ejectment.
This principle is based on the doctrine of agency and one co-owner filing a suit for eviction against the tenant does so on his behalf in his own right as well as an agent of the other co-owners.

On that count, the objection of the respondent regarding non-impleadment of other LRs of Harjeet Singh stands rejected and as the tenanted portion has nothing to do with Mohan Bir Singh after separation of their shares, the question of RC ARC No. 23/2023 Inderjeet Kaur Vs. Anil Kumar Singhal Page no. 10 of 25 his impleadment in the present proceedings does not arise at all.

entities.text: Inderjeet Kaur Vs. Anil Kumar Singhal
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The settlement order relied upon by the petitioner is sufficient to evidence petitioner's co-ownership over the property in the present eviction petition and contrary to what the respondent has alleged, she need not prove her title to the hilt as is required under Transfer of Property Act.
Infact, she only needs to prove that she is more than a tenant for the purpose of the present eviction proceedings.

There is also no requirement in law for any notice of attornment to be served by her upon the tenant as being the successor of the previous owner, she would step into his shoes with regard to all the rights and liabilities in the tenanted premises.
13. In view of the above, petitioner has been able to successfully establish that she is the co-owner of the tenanted premises.
Every owner is also a landlord though converse may not be true.
Thus, it is held that there exists a landlord-tenant relationship between the parties.
The denial of the respondent in that regard has no value in the eyes of law.

He is also not competent to question the family settlement arrived between the parties (see "Rishal Singh Vs. Bohat Ram & Ors", 2014 (144)
DRJ 633).

sentences.text: Hence, neither shop No. 4 nor the above floors are available with the petitioner for being used for her business.

Besides even if upper floors were available with the petitioner, it is a matter of common knowledge that the upper floors are generally not commercially viable and consumers and patrons of the market are reluctant to walk into the same and are more prone to walk into a shop on the ground floor.

Thus, even though there is no construction made on the upper floors of the property in question which has fallen into petitioner's share and there is only a terrace,
but even if some space were available, as held in catena of case, availability of upper floors above the tenanted premises on the ground floor could not have been said to be alternative suitable accommodation.

16. In short, a comprehensive reading of the site plan filed by the respondent with the order of the High Court (supra) shows that Harjeet Singh got the left side of the property no. F14/60-61 while Mohan Bir got the right side.
The parties/brothers to the settlement have already acted upon the settlement and taken possession of their respective portions.
Respondent has not brought anything on record to show that same is not the case or that even the properties shown to be vacant have fallen into petitioner's share.

Thus, there is no reason to disbelieve that in view of Order dated 05.04.2019, the right side portion which includes the shop no. 4 alongwith the floors above it are in Mohan Bir's share and hence, cannot be utilized by the petitioner for her requirements so as to be termed as an alternative suitable RC ARC No. 23/2023 Inderjeet Kaur Vs. sentences.text: 17. That leaves us with shop no. 2 on the ground floor, stated to be admeasuring 10' X 16', also shown in red color in the site plan Annexure R-XVII.

Although the same has fallen into petitioner's share, she states that the ceiling of this room is low, having a height of not more than 3-4 ft., because of an indent caused due to a staircase above it.
Therefore, it cannot be used for running any kind of business except maybe for a cloud kitchen/fast food delivery joint or for storage.
There seems to be merit in the submissions of the petitioner and same is also substantiated by the photographs filed by the both the sides.
The staircase passing above the said room has hardly left any space in the same and would also be hazardous for the occupants, if used.
Thus, its existence or availability is of no consequence to the present proceedings.
18. Besides it hardly requires any re-iteration that a tenant cannot dictate terms to the landlord as to how and in what manner she should utilize her own property.

However, the photographs filed by the respondent makes it clear that same is a residential property with the name plate "Harbhajan Niwas" affixed at its entrance.

A residential property by no stretch RC ARC No. 23/2023 Inderjeet Kaur Vs. Hamilton Road, Kashmere Gate, Delhi of which approximately 400 square yards is lying vacant.
The suitability of any accommodation has to be assessed in respect of the felt need of the landlord.
Petitioner is residing in Model Town and wants to run her business also from Model Town.
The tenanted premises is situated in Model Town and thus in close proximity to her residence and more convenient to her.

The motive for running any kind of business is obviously profit and if the petitioner considers the tenanted premises to be more profitable and convenient for her requirements, then the respondent while occupying her property cannot ask her to move to some other place, which is less convenient, farther and not ideal for her requirements.
It need not be reiterated that petitioner is the best judge of her requirements.

Thus, neither of the properties mentioned by the respondent can be termed as an alternative suitable accommodation and apart from above, respondent has not been able to show availability of any other accommodation with the petitioner.
Respondent's remaining objection that the petitioner failed to state in express terms in the petition that she does not have an alternative suitable accommodation is also without merit.

Petitioner has throughout averred in her petition that only the tenanted premises is most suited for her requirements and in her reply to the leave to defend application, she has expressly stated that she does not have an alternative suitable accommodation for her requirements.
Therefore, it cannot be said that such pleading is missing.
Pleadings have to be read meaningfully and a hyper-technical approach has to be avoided.

The objections of the respondent in this regard accordingly stand rejected and it is held that petitioner has been able to establish the unavailability of an alternative suitable accommodation with her for her requirements.

C. BONAFIDE REQUIREMENT 24.
Respondent has argued that the need of the petitioner is not genuine.

He states that petitioner is around 64 years of age, inexperienced and it would be preposterous to expect that she could venture into a new business at such an advanced age that too from a small shop admeasuring 200 sq feet which is currently being used as a grocery/departmental store by the respondent.
25. Petitioner is a widowed lady who wants to run her own business and stand on her own feet.
Merely because she is 64 years of age would not debar her from venturing into new avenues in life.
Any person can have a fresh start at any stage and age in life and the legislature has not put a number on the same.
It is petitioner's fundamental right to enter into a vocation or business of her choice irrespective of her age and respondent is no one to say otherwise.
Her lack of previous experience would also not come in her way and same is quite immaterial while deciding her bonafides.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is trite that in an eviction petition for bonafide requirement, leave to defend is to be granted only when the tenant is able to raise any triable issue which can be adjudicated only on the consideration of additional evidence.
The tenant must disclose such a prima facie case as would dis-entitle the landlord from obtaining an eviction order, lest an eviction order has to be passed.
Even if Mohan Bir Singh had been collecting rent from the tenant of the property, he could only have done so in the capacity of a co-landlord/co-owner as the property in question continued to be joint RC ARC No.
23/2023 Inderjeet Kaur Vs. Anil Kumar Singhal Page no. 9 of 25 until the separation of shares by the settlement order.
However, post the settlement, the tenanted premises came into the exclusive share of petitioner's husband and by law of succession, ultimately in the share of petitioner and her children.
Inderjeet Kaur vs Anil Kumar Singhal on 7 March, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/120685659/
5 12.
As regards the competence of the petitioner to file the present eviction proceedings, once it is held that she is atleast a co- owner of the tenanted premises, being one of the legal heirs of Harjeet Singh, she is entitled to file the present eviction petition without impleading the other co-owners i.e.
her children.
This principle is based on the doctrine of agency and one co-owner filing a suit for eviction against the tenant does so on his behalf in his own right as well as an agent of the other co-owners.
Thus, it is held that there exists a landlord-tenant relationship between the parties.
The denial of the respondent in that regard has no value in the eyes of law.
He is also not competent to question the family settlement arrived between the parties (see "Rishal Singh Vs. Bohat Ram & Ors", 2014 (144)
DRJ 633).

Thus, even though there is no construction made on the upper floors of the property in question which has fallen into petitioner's share and there is only a terrace,
but even if some space were available, as held in catena of case, availability of upper floors above the tenanted premises on the ground floor could not have been said to be alternative suitable accommodation.
